title: system-one-mini
oneliner: I generated a dataset and trained a tiny decision model. Perfect on familiar wording, 44.5% on new wording, still 97% sure.
role: Dataset generator, training, evaluation and release, on one RTX 3060.
status_note: Experiment, finished. What it taught is built into nibble.
question: For repeated, fixed-format decisions about an agent's state, can one small shared encoder with typed heads replace asking a generative model each question?
tried: One DistilBERT encoder with five classifier heads: task complete, should retry, failure source (5 options), next action (5 options), evidence sufficient. It generates zero tokens; software maps the logits to legal option names.
Baselines: TF-IDF with logistic regression, and SmolLM2-360M asked zero-shot.
A follow-up round of candidates run in parallel: more writing styles, weighted loss, LoRA, deeper heads. Deeper heads won.
data: Fully synthetic and deterministic: a state machine creates each latent situation and its labels first, then a renderer writes it as text. Seed 1729. No teacher model, no API, no LLM paraphrasing.

The domain: four components (code, environment, test fixture, dependency) are each restored to known-good on a failing snapshot; exactly one clearing repair names the failure source. Error strings and recent edits are distractors.
20,000 training states with 5 labels each (100,000 decisions), plus 2,000-state splits for validation, calibration, familiar-wording test and unseen-wording test, and 600 out-of-domain probes.
Version 2 spread the same states over 12 writing styles (ticket, terminal, Slack thread, stack trace, PR review...). A final style, case_review, was written after model selection and evaluated once.
model: DistilBERT base, 66.4M parameters (69.3M for the released deep-head model). Full fine-tune, AdamW 3e-5, batch 16, 3 epochs, BF16.
376.7 seconds of training for 20,000 states, peaking at 1.7 GB of GPU memory.
results: Familiar wording: 100% accurate. Unseen wording: 44.51%, with mean confidence still at 97.19%.
Failure source on unseen wording: 21% accurate at 99.6% confidence. In 200 pairs where only the fix changed, the prediction changed 0 times.
The final deep-head model scored 86.25% on the post-selection style; next action, a policy choice rather than a fact, stayed weakest at 62.8%.
Speed held up: 5 decisions in 4.95 ms p50, and encoding the state once for 50 questions is about 42x faster than encoding it 50 times.
learned: 100% on one generator's templates measures interpolation, not understanding. Keep a wording holdout separate from dev.
Confidence is not a safety signal: report NLL and calibration next to accuracy.
More writing styles did not help monotonically. Surface variety is not semantic variety.
Fixed heads can't take a new question. A decision layer needs the question and the options in its input.
became_text: nibble keeps the one real win (encode the state once, ask many questions) and replaces fixed heads with a question-conditioned pointer head. It trains on real logged decisions with outcomes, uses synthetic data only as a supplement, and refits temperature per domain.

title: system-a
oneliner: I mined real coding-agent traces into a dataset and fine-tuned a 421M model to guess the agent's next tool.
role: Trace-to-dataset pipeline, local trainer, evaluation and release bundle, on one RTX 3060.
status_note: Experiment, finished. Its rules are built into nibble.
question: Can an open typed-decision model (Laya) learn an agent's choices from real traces, trained locally on a 12 GB card?
tried: Reflex: a local CLI that runs the public Laya typed-decision checkpoint on an agent state and typed questions, offline.
A local trainer for Laya's RLCD objective plus cross-entropy, adapted from a 2x T4 recipe to one 12 GB card.
Two data paths abandoned on evidence: one trace set had no real tool results, another kept a 20-point bias toward three tools even at 1,024 tokens.
data: Trace2Decision turns public coding-agent traces (a CC BY 4.0 set) into state, question and gold records. One record is one whole assistant turn; the label is the tool category the agent actually used next.
1,821 turns in, 1,313 kept. Dropped: 224 with an unresolved earlier tool call, 208 no-call turns without a clear finish, 76 that mixed categories.
Split 1,051 / 140 / 122 by task group, so no trajectory, task or rendered state crosses splits.
Two of the six classes (other tool, respond or finish) ended with zero examples in every split.
model: Laya: a ModernBERT-large encoder plus a small option scorer, 421M parameters.
RLCD plus 6-way cross-entropy, micro-batch 1 with 64-step accumulation, FP16, 4 epochs. One seed: 767 s of training at 9.52 GiB peak, under an 11.5 GiB budget.
results: First, a positive control: the public specialist beat its base 68.0% to 35.5%, so the evaluator worked. My own trainer then lifted a control task from 36.0% to 70.5%.
On dev, Laya beat a TF-IDF baseline on macro-F1 (0.445 vs 0.293) and lost badly on NLL (3.41 vs 0.95): its wrong answers came at above 0.9999 confidence.
The main run died at the end: the disk filled up while saving the checkpoint.
learned: Reproduce a known positive control before trusting your own trainer.
Every option needs real examples in train and dev, or it isn't a capability.
Ship a dumb baseline and report NLL and Brier next to accuracy.
It drifted: meant to pick options, it learned to copy one harness's habits. Label decisions by outcome, not by what a big model picked.
became_text: nibble carries the evidence table and the positive-control-first rule, and labels its records by outcome. bonfire took the operations lesson: per-call timeouts, logged retries and a disk check before long writes.

title: benchlet
oneliner: A small benchmark with hidden tests. The agent passed every visible test and still failed 2 of 7 tasks.
role: Task design, hidden evaluators, runner and the pilot run.
status_note: Experiment, finished. bonfire uses it as its eval corpus.
question: Does orchestrating several agents beat one agent at the same total budget? First you need tasks that can tell.
tried: 16 small Python maintenance tasks, each with a starter, visible tests, a sealed hidden evaluator, a reference and an audit.
A runner that grades each task on a fresh copy with a fixed hash seed, timezone and locale.
A protocol: paired, task-level comparison against one direct agent at equal total budget.
data: Hand-curated, not generated: a 125-idea pool cut to 16 by four reviews (coverage, deterministic oracle, discrimination, adversarial validity).
results: A blind pilot with one fresh agent on 7 tasks: 7 of 7 passed every visible test; 2 of 7 failed hidden tests (a recursion limit on a 1,100-node chain, one missed validation).
The orchestration comparison itself was never run.
learned: Visible tests passing is not the same as working.
Compare a loop against one agent at equal total budget, with the task as the unit.
became_text: bonfire pins benchlet by commit as its external eval corpus, with the equal-budget rule and the pilot table as its first target. playdough keeps the idea as a held-back playability check the generating agent never sees.

title: gauntlet
oneliner: A propose, evaluate, criticize, verify loop over git worktrees. 67 tests, never run on a real model.
role: Design and build of the harness, store and tests.
status_note: Experiment, finished. Its loop design lives on in bonfire.
question: Can a small, model-agnostic loop improve a file against an executable contract, with critics and an independent verifier?
tried: A CLI loop: propose, snapshot, evaluate deterministically, criticize with fresh read-only critics, verify in a separate worktree, select, then mutate or reset.
A durable store with a per-run lock, atomic state and an append-only event log, so a run resumes after a crash.
A scripted self-test: one worker, one worker plus review, and three parallel workers on a toy 100-point contract.
results: In the scripted test, one worker stopped at 75; review plus revision and three parallel workers both reached 100.
Those were scripted workers: no model calls, so it says nothing about real agents. Most commits went into recovery edge cases before a single real loop ran.
learned: A critic's finding is a claim; only a fresh verifier makes it a fact.
Run one real loop before hardening recovery.
Build on a durable runtime instead of writing your own git state machine.
became_text: bonfire is the harness built for gauntlet loops: the loop phases, the finding schema and verify rule, the durable store, the restart test and the worktree helper all moved there, on a durable runtime instead of a hand-rolled one.

title: primitive
oneliner: A claim graph of what 10 open-source repos can do, where every claim points to source lines.
role: Ontology, curation and the query CLI.
status_note: Experiment, finished. Its card schema is in mise en place.
question: Can an agent ask 'what can I build this with?' and get answers backed by evidence instead of memory?
tried: An ontology and a SQLite claim graph over 10 repos pinned by commit: swarm, pydantic-ai, llama.cpp, ollama, bubbletea, duckdb, prefect, ripgrep, FFmpeg, three.js.
A query CLI for capabilities, alternatives, primitives, licenses, components and provenance.
I dropped the project, capability, primitive, component chain: a reusable component became a query, not an entity.
data: Hand-curated claim bundles: 48 components, 46 concepts, 215 source artifacts, 231 claims and 720 evidence links. A script checks every quoted excerpt against git.
results: Every claim traced to source. But the whole first version went into identity and evidence, and none of it was about what I actually wanted to build.
learned: Start with a flat list of cards; add structure only when a query needs it.
Licenses belong to each asset, not each repo (three.js is MIT; its example assets are not).
became_text: mise en place uses its capability contract (inputs, outputs, effects, preconditions, postconditions, hard qualifiers, non-goals) as the primitive-card schema, with a license field per asset. playdough keeps the per-asset license rule.

title: precision-canvas
oneliner: A design canvas that became a 473-capability spec before it drew a single pixel.
role: Spec, invariants and the conformance harness.
status_note: Experiment, finished. napkin is the canvas it was meant to be.
question: What would a canvas for components need to guarantee, before building it?
tried: A frozen spec with 473 capabilities and 14 invariants, and a five-stage verify command with CI.
Reference packages for the document, geometry, identity, storage and transactions.
A transaction model: batched edits, dry runs through the same planner, attributed commits, undo as a new transaction.
results: The spec grew to 620 KB. Every change needed a decision record, and no editor or renderer was ever built.
learned: Write only the spec the live demo needs.
One mutation path for every writer, human or agent, attributed and undoable.
Plain files and git first; prove you need more before building it.
became_text: napkin is the canvas built the other way round: working first. It kept five invariants, the agent-surface and code-component checklists, and the condensed transaction model.
